/conditions/juvenile-arthritis/symptoms.title: Juvenile Arthritis Symptoms: Early Signs & GP Advice
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis/symptoms.description: Early signs of juvenile arthritis, common symptoms and when to see your GP. Plain-English UK guidance based on NHS and NICE advice. Not a diagnosis.
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis/symptoms.question: Juvenile arthritis symptoms
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis/symptoms.answer: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis can cause persistent joint pain, swelling, stiffness or changes in how a child moves. Inflammation can affect joint function and interfere with everyday play and activities. Arrange a GP assessment for a child with joint problems rather than assuming they are ordinary growing pains.
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis/symptoms.bodyHtml:
A child with joint symptoms: when to get help

Arrange a GP assessment for a child with joint problems or a limp with no obvious cause. Do not wait two or six weeks before asking for help. A duration used to classify arthritis is not a waiting period for parents.

Emergency help

For a child with a limp, call 999 or go to A&E if they develop sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, cannot put weight on their leg, have a leg that has changed shape, feel generally unwell with a high temperature or shivering, have severe lower tummy pain, or their symptoms get worse. Do not drive to A&E; ask someone to drive or call 999 for an ambulance.

Eye symptoms and screening

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 advice for eye pain, sensitivity to light, very red eyes or a change in vision. If your child cannot see, go to A&E or call 999. Do not wait for the next screening appointment. JIA-related uveitis can also occur without symptoms, so keep all specialist eye-screening appointments.

Exercise must fit the child

Activity advice here is for a child whose condition has been assessed. A new unexplained limp, sudden pain or inability to bear weight needs assessment, not an adult exercise programme. The paediatric physiotherapist should tailor activities, loads and repetitions to the child's joints, age, abilities and treatment. During an assessed JIA flare, the team may recommend low-impact activity and avoiding contact or high-impact sport. Follow the child's own plan, including after a procedure.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis can cause persistent joint pain, swelling, stiffness or changes in how a child moves. Inflammation can affect joint function and interfere with everyday play and activities. Arrange a GP assessment for a child with joint problems rather than assuming they are ordinary growing pains.

Common symptoms of juvenile arthritis

  • Joint pain, swelling or warmth: seek assessment rather than waiting six weeks
  • Morning stiffness or a limp on waking
  • A reluctance to use a particular limb or joint
  • Unexplained fevers, rashes, or fatigue (in systemic JIA)
  • Eye inflammation (uveitis) — often without symptoms, so screening is essential
  • Growth delay or limb-length differences in long-standing disease

When to see your GP

Arrange a GP assessment for a child with joint problems or an unexplained limp. Do not wait a few weeks or use the six-week JIA classification period as a waiting rule. Follow the emergency and eye advice above when relevant.

Juvenile arthritis treatment is planned by a paediatric rheumatology team and may include medicines, physiotherapy and practical support. Controlling inflammation helps protect joint function while a child grows and develops. Follow the individual treatment and monitoring plan, and discuss changes in symptoms or activity with the team.

Treatment approaches

Individual medicine plan

The paediatric rheumatology team chooses treatment for the child and arranges monitoring. Do not use adult doses or change treatment from this page.

Specialist follow-up

Review symptoms, treatment effects and any new concerns with the child's team.

Steroid joint injections

Targeted treatment for individual swollen joints.

NSAIDs

Used for symptom control alongside disease-modifying treatment.

Paediatric physiotherapy

Maintains range of motion and supports normal physical development.

Uveitis screening

Regular eye checks by ophthalmology to detect silent eye inflammation.

Children with juvenile arthritis can benefit from activity adapted to their symptoms, abilities and treatment plan. Suitable movement helps maintain joint mobility and muscle strength while supporting participation in play. Ask the paediatric physiotherapy team about appropriate activities and how to adjust them when symptoms change.

Key benefits

  • Maintains joint range of motion
  • Builds strength to protect affected joints
  • Supports normal growth and bone development
  • Improves confidence and social participation
  • Reduces the deconditioning that comes with chronic illness

Children with juvenile arthritis need a varied, age-appropriate diet rather than restrictive arthritis diets or unverified supplements. Adequate energy and nutrients support growth, muscle function and bone health during treatment. Discuss poor appetite, weight changes or supplement questions with the paediatric team or a registered dietitian.

Foods to favour

  • Calcium-rich foods (dairy or fortified alternatives) every day
  • Age-appropriate foods and portions, with advice from the paediatric team
  • Variety of fruit and vegetables
  • Wholegrains and pulses
  • Lean protein for growth and muscle development

Foods to limit

  • Sugary drinks and ultra-processed snacks
  • Excess fast food
  • Do not remove food groups or start a supplement without paediatric or dietitian advice

faqs.q: Should my child follow an adult arthritis diet?
faqs.a: Do not apply adult weight-loss plans or restrictive arthritis diets to a growing child. NHS Eatwell proportions do not apply below age two; children move towards them after age two. Ask the paediatric team or registered dietitian about age-appropriate food, growth, appetite and any need for supplements.
No. Do not replace the child's prescribed treatment with a supplement or exclusion diet. Check any product with the child's pharmacist or paediatric team first.

faqs.q: What if eating or growth becomes a concern?
faqs.a: Contact the paediatric team about poor appetite, weight changes or concerns about growth. They can assess the cause and whether dietitian support is needed.

What is juvenile arthritis?

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) covers a group of autoimmune conditions that cause joint inflammation in children and young people under the age of 16. "Idiopathic" simply means the cause is unknown.

A paediatric rheumatology team assesses and treats JIA. The outlook and treatment vary between children. This guide cannot predict a child's long-term joint function.

Symptoms

  • Joint pain, swelling or stiffness: seek assessment rather than waiting six weeks
  • Limping — particularly first thing in the morning
  • Reluctance to use a hand, knee or other joint
  • Unexplained fevers or rashes (systemic JIA)
  • Swollen lymph nodes
  • Eye inflammation (uveitis) can be silent; attend screening even without eye symptoms
  • Slowed growth or unequal limb length in long-standing disease

Causes

  • In JIA the immune system attacks the joints; why this happens is not fully understood
  • JIA is not something a child catches from another person
  • Nothing a child or parent did or did not do caused their JIA

Treatment and support

  • An individual treatment and monitoring plan from paediatric rheumatology
  • Medicines to control inflammation, selected and monitored for the child
  • Joint steroid injections when the specialist team recommends them
  • Paediatric physiotherapy, occupational therapy and pain-management support
  • Specialist eye screening even when the eyes look and feel normal

Food and growth

Children with JIA need a balanced diet that supports growth, bone density and a healthy weight. There is no specific JIA diet.

  • Plenty of fruit, vegetables and whole grains
  • Calcium-rich foods (milk, yoghurt, fortified plant drinks) and vitamin D
  • Discuss food choices and any supplements with the paediatric team
  • Limit sugary drinks and ultra-processed snacks
  • Speak to a paediatric dietitian if your child is on long-term steroids

Activity and school

Regular, age-appropriate movement helps maintain strength, flexibility and bone health. Children with JIA can usually take part in PE with sensible adaptations.

  • Swimming — gentle on joints and great for full-body strength
  • Cycling, scootering and dancing
  • Physiotherapy-led stretches for affected joints
  • Avoid heavy contact sports during active flares
  • Talk to school PE staff so activities can be adapted, not avoided

faqs.q: What are the first signs of arthritis in a child?
faqs.a: Look out for limping, a swollen or stiff joint, or reluctance to use a limb. Arrange a GP assessment for joint problems or an unexplained limp. Do not wait two or six weeks. Use the emergency advice on this page for sudden hip, knee or thigh pain, inability to bear weight or an unwell child.

faqs.q: Is juvenile arthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: No. JIA is its own group of conditions. Some forms behave similarly to rheumatoid arthritis, but JIA also includes types not seen in adults, such as systemic JIA (Still's disease).

faqs.q: Will my child grow out of JIA?
faqs.a: The course varies between children. Ask the paediatric rheumatology team about your child's condition, treatment goals and follow-up. Improvement is not a reason to stop treatment or eye screening without the team's advice.

faqs.q: Why does my child need eye checks?
faqs.a: JIA can cause silent eye inflammation (uveitis) that, if missed, can damage sight. Regular slit-lamp checks by an ophthalmologist are essential.

faqs.q: Can my child still play sport?
faqs.a: When JIA is assessed and well controlled, children can often take part in activities they enjoy. The paediatric physiotherapist and school should agree adaptations for the individual child, particularly during a flare or after a procedure. Do not apply an adult exercise programme to a child.
